recipe.history:
The American diner burger — chili, onion rings, jalapeños, American cheese, sesame bun — is rock and roll made edible: loud, indulgent, assembled without apology, and structured around the principle that more is more. Its cultural roots run through every roadside diner, truck-stop grill, and dive bar kitchen that has ever existed in the United States, gathering influence from the chili-burger traditions of the American Southwest, where a ladle of beef chili over a patty became a regional staple at stands and diners in New Mexico, Texas, and California by the 1930s and 1940s. Chili itself has an origin story as contested as any in American food — San Antonio's chili queens sold their spiced beef stews in the plazas of the city from the 1870s onward, and the combination of chili peppers, beef, and fat became one of the defining flavor profiles of the American South and West. Onion rings, meanwhile, arrived in American diners by the 1930s — a Crisco advertisement from 1933 is often cited as the first printed onion ring recipe — and the combination of their sweet, onion-forward interior and their shatteringly crispy fried exterior made them the natural companion to any burger that wanted to announce itself as a serious proposition.

Jalapeños crossed into mainstream American burger culture from the Tex-Mex tradition, carried northward and eastward by Mexican-American communities and by the relentless spread of Tex-Mex cuisine through the twentieth century. By the 1980s, the jalapeño burger had become a fixture of casual dining chains, and its combination of capsaicin heat, bright vegetable flavor, and pickling acidity made it one of the most durable burger innovations of the modern era. The Radio No You Didn't Burger brings all of these elements together — chili, onion rings, jalapeños, American cheese, sesame bun — in a deliberately maximalist tribute to the diner-burger tradition at its most theatrical. Like a power chord, every ingredient hits at once.

I have a memory of a specific diner in central Texas — I was driving cross-country, it was July, the air conditioning was making a noise like a dying animal — where I ordered the chili burger from a laminated menu that had not been updated since approximately 1987. The chili came from a vat behind the counter that had clearly been simmering since the previous Tuesday, and the onion rings came from a fryer basket that never fully cooled down, and the jalapeños were from a jar, and the whole thing was assembled in about forty seconds by a cook who clearly had better things to do than appreciate the beauty of what she was making. It was one of the best burgers I have ever eaten. The Radio No You Didn't Burger is my attempt to reconstruct that moment: the loud, unapologetic, everything-at-once diner classic, made with slightly more care than the original but without losing any of its fundamental rock-and-roll energy.

If any burger in this collection can make the case for medium rare purely on structural grounds, it is this one. The chili is warm and liquid, the onion rings are crispy and slightly greasy, the jalapeños are acid-sharp, and the American cheese melts over everything into a glossy orange film. Beneath all of this — beneath the weight and heat and grease of the toppings — the patty must retain its own identity. A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit has a texture and a presence that can stand up to all of this: it is firm enough to be the foundation of the construction, yielding enough to be a pleasure to bite through, and juicy enough to combine with the chili rather than be overshadowed by it. A well-done patty is a puck in a pile of toppings. A medium-rare patty is the center of gravity around which everything else organizes. Medium rare is not a preference here. It is structural necessity.
ingredients: 1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
2 large yellow onions, sliced into 1/2-inch rounds, rings separated
240ml cold sparkling water or cold beer
softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Make the sesame buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the stand mixer bowl with dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix, then add butter gradually. Knead on medium-high 8 minutes until smooth. Rise until doubled, 1 to 1.5 hours. Divide into 6 portions, shape, proof 40 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Egg wash, sesame seeds, bake 18 to 20 minutes. Cool.

2. Make the chili: Heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Brown the ground beef, breaking it up, until cooked through. Drain excess fat, leaving about 1 tablespoon. Add onion and cook until softened, 5 minutes. Add garlic and all spices; cook 1 minute until fragrant. Add diced tomatoes, beans, and beef broth. Bring to a boil, reduce heat, and simmer uncovered for 30 to 40 minutes until thick and deeply flavored. Season with salt and pepper. Keep warm.

3. Make the onion rings: Soak onion rings in buttermilk for 30 minutes. In a bowl, whisk flour, cornmeal, baking powder, salt, paprika, garlic powder, and cayenne. Just before frying, whisk in cold sparkling water until a thick batter forms. Heat 3 inches of neutral oil in a heavy pot to 365°F (185°C). Drain onion rings from buttermilk, letting excess drip off. Dip in batter, let excess drip off, and fry in batches until golden and crispy, 3 to 4 minutes. Drain on a rack and season with salt immediately.
4. Make the diner sauce: Whisk mayonnaise, ketchup, yellow mustard, hot sauce, and relish together until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Form the patties: Divide beef into 6 portions (about 150g each). Shape into 4-inch patties, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Season generously with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

6. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat until smoking. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes on the first side. Flip and immediately lay 2 slices of American cheese on each patty. Cook 2 to 2.5 more minutes. Add a splash of water and cover to steam-melt the cheese for 30 seconds. The internal temperature must reach 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — medium rare, the only correct doneness. Rest patties on a rack for 3 minutes.
7. Toast the buns: Butter the cut sides and toast in the skillet butter-side down over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.

8. Assemble: Spread diner sauce on both bun halves. Place the double-American-cheese-covered patty on the bottom bun. Spoon a generous ladle of hot chili directly over the patty and cheese. Lay 4 to 6 pickled jalapeño slices over the chili. Stack 2 to 3 crispy onion rings on top. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately — this burger does not wait.
